sentences.text: Callisto, the outermost and the quietest of the four Galilean moons.
Its surface is the most densely cratered surface in the Solar System; it has barely changed for 4 billion years.
Because it is far from Jupiter, it is not affected by tidal heating and remains outside the radiation belts.
This makes it the safest candidate for a crewed base in the future.
There are also clues that an ocean may exist beneath it.
Europa, the most promising destination in the search for life.
Beneath its smooth ice shell, a global saltwater ocean holding twice as much water as all the oceans on Earth is thought to exist.
The brown lines on the surface are places where the ice cracks and water from below seeps upward.
NASA's Europa Clipper spacecraft was launched in 2024 and, in 2030, with about 50 close flybys, will investigate whether this ocean is habitable.
Ganymede, the largest moon in the Solar System.
It is even larger than the planet Mercury.
It is the only known moon with its own magnetic field; this field forms a small bubble inside Jupiter's and creates auroras at its poles.
Its surface is of two different ages: dark, cratered old regions and light-colored, grooved younger regions.
Beneath its ice shell, it has an ocean too.
The European Space Agency's JUICE spacecraft will enter orbit around it in 2031.
Io, the most volcanic world in the Solar System.
It is constantly squeezed and stretched between the gravity of Jupiter and the other moons; this tidal heating melts its interior.
There are more than 400 active volcanoes on its surface, and some of them hurl lava hundreds of kilometers high.
The yellow, orange, and red colors come from sulfur and sulfur compounds.
Its surface is renewed so quickly that it has almost no impact craters.
Finally, let's look at Juno.
This NASA spacecraft entered orbit around Jupiter in July 2016.
It is the first spacecraft to operate on solar power this far from the Sun; its three giant panels take up as much space as a basketball court.
To protect itself from radiation, it travels in a long, elliptical orbit that passes over the poles, and on each pass it flies a few thousand kilometers above the clouds.
It discovered giant cyclones at Jupiter's poles and showed that Jupiter's core is larger and more diffuse than had been thought.
Our tour of Jupiter ends here.
Welcome to the Jupiter system.
This giant is almost like a small solar system: more than 95 moons orbit around it.

The planet is so large that 1,300 Earths can fit inside it, and its powerful magnetic field is the largest structure in the Solar System; if it could be seen in the sky, it would appear larger than the full Moon.
In 1610, Galileo discovered its four large moons with his small telescope, and this became the first evidence that not everything revolves around Earth.
Now we will visit those four moons in turn.
